On coding agents it beats Opus 5.5, 68 to 66. For OpenAI, the model isn't even the scary part. Meta's Muse app hit No. 1 on the US App Store 10 days after launch, and 73% of new users came back the next day, nearly double ChatGPT's rate. The lab everyone mocked 18 months ago now outscores OpenAI. And it already has over 3 billion people using its apps every day. https://t.co/Kljrenyq94

I was in their Mission Bay office, in the summer of 2025, the night before the launch of GPT-5. There was a certain buzz to the building. The overhead lights burned like stage lights, and people seemed to walk the warm rusts and browns of its halls just a little faster than usual. Even the gravity felt heavier—as if the sheer size of the following day’s launch had drawn the rest of the world into its orbit. This made what I had come to say a little awkward. Every, the company I run, had begun to build a reputation for testing new AI models on real work and explaining what they could—and couldn’t—do. OpenAI had given us access to GPT-5 about a month before launch so we could help them understand the model’s strengths and weaknesses and publish our Vibe Check—a detailed review—on launch day. Ten of us had spent a week in a house in upstate New York for a team retreat, eating and working together at one long wooden table and gathering on a couch in front of a big screen to test the long-awaited model. We were especially excited to try it for coding, where AI was advancing fastest. But while we liked it for everyday use, our reaction to it in Codex was muted. Today, Codex is the centerpiece of OpenAI’s comeback—the product that has swallowed ChatGPT from the inside and become the foundation for everything the company is building next. But that summer it was still a scrappy effort to build an AI software engineer. A version launched in the cloud a few months earlier hadn’t found product-market fit, and the team was mid-pivot to a new version that ran on a developer’s computer in their terminal and in their code editor. In Codex, GPT-5 was fast, and it seemed smart. One of our most technical engineers, Naveen Naidu, had used it to track down a mysterious freeze in his voice dictation app Monologue that had stumped him for days. But it also seemed to stop too early, as if it were overly wary of stepping outside the bounds of what it was allowed to do. It felt designed to be used as a pair programmer. As a team, we were moving beyond step-by-step collaboration with AI models. Using Anthropic’s terminal agent, Claude Code, a group of us led by Kieran Klaassen had started handing entire tasks to Opus 4 and walking away until a finished feature—or sometimes an entire app—came back. With minimal help from an engineer, staff writer Katie Parrott built and deployed her own AI content management system in a few days. It had some bugs, but building it would previously have been out of reach. Next to Opus 4 inside Claude Code, GPT-5 inside Codex felt boxed in. Sharing what we’d found in our testing had brought me to a conference room in OpenAI’s office with Lindsay McCallum from the communications team and Alexander Embiricos from the Codex team. I sensed that McCallum, who has a keen radar for vibe shifts in the market, had set up the conversation so I could explain to Embiricos why I suddenly wouldn’t shut up about this new way of working. McCallum was typing with intense focus on her laptop across the conference table from me. Embiricos sat beside me, coding while he talked, which I took as a good sign. He was rushing to finish a GPT-5 release feature that would let the agent pause and ask a human for permission to access files or run commands outside its sandbox. “With Claude Code, you just let it rip,” I told Embiricos. “GPT-5 feels a little timid—like it’s held back by the sandbox and it seems afraid to use its own power.” The tapping of McCallum’s keys slowed. “Tell Alexander about this new engineering workflow you have,” I remember her saying without looking up from her laptop. Embiricos swiveled his chair to focus fully on me. “We don’t even really look at the code anymore,” I began. But I blushed as I said it. I felt ridiculous explaining agentic delegation to Embiricos, of all people—building an autonomous coding agent was his job. I also wasn’t sure, at the time, that our engineering approach would work beyond our tiny team. A Slack ping lit up Embiricos’s screen and broke the sudden quiet of the conference room. He muted his computer and pushed its lid three-quarters shut—just enough to keep his Codex agent thinking. Leaving Mission Bay that night, I wondered if OpenAI was building the perfect tool for a dying workflow. Today, Codex and ChatGPT for Work combined have 40 million weekly active users. evidence.title: I'm thoroughly Dots-pilled. Still a fan of Muse, but probably 75-80% of my AI requests now go throug
evidence.text: I'm thoroughly Dots-pilled. Still a fan of Muse, but probably 75-80% of my AI requests now go through Dots. The primary exception: learning things in chat. For that, GPT-6 Instant with Dynamic UI is unmatched. Just incredible. Some recent Dots work and personal tasks: - Build and update a Spanish vocabulary app - Maintain a document on AI comparisons - Execute tasks I delegate directly from Slack - Monitor threads in Slack and summarize responses - Research a contact and write a brief for a call - Analyze token data and make me a deck to share - Monitor token consumption, alert me if needed - Respond to comments in Pages in Space You might say: "Dude, ChatGPT could do a lot of that already." True. But I no longer have to think about all these threads individually. I just keep firing stuff at my Dots from wherever I am. ChatGPT, Slack, reading a Page in Space. I just throw stuff at it, and it does it, and sometimes it proactively just does stuff based on what it thinks I'd find valuable. I was skeptical when this launched because it's nowhere near as consumer-friendly as Muse. But I think that's part of why OpenAI launched this first to business and pro-tier users. We're willing to suffer a bit for extra capability. I'm starting to see some of the advantages now, and the product also continues to get more polished. Bullish.

evidence.title: Google pays $250K bounty for AI-assisted Chrome exploit built in six days
evidence.text: Google pays $250K bounty for AI-assisted Chrome exploit built in six days October 14, 2026 By Bill Mann — Leave a Comment XLinkedInRedditFacebookShare XBOW has disclosed an AI-assisted Chrome exploit that could let attackers run code on a Windows computer simply by getting its user to visit a malicious webpage. Google has fixed all three vulnerabilities used in the chain and awarded the researchers a $250,000 bounty. The company published its findings on October 13, describing how researcher Brendan Dolan-Gavitt and AI agents built the exploit chain between August 2 and August 7. The effort used OpenAI’s publicly available GPT-5.6 Sol model and approximately $40,000 in compute over six days. XBOW develops AI-driven offensive security tools that search for exploitable weaknesses. This project extended its work beyond web applications to Chrome, whose layered defenses are designed to prevent compromised web content from reaching the underlying operating system. Three bugs crossed Chrome’s security boundaries Dolan-Gavitt’s technical report describes a chain combining flaws in V8, Chrome’s JavaScript engine; its animated-WebP image decoder; and Crashpad, its crash-reporting component. The first flaw involved V8’s Maglev optimizing compiler and gave the exploit access to memory within the engine’s sandbox. The image-decoding flaw then allowed it to cross that boundary by changing image data after the decoder had cached information about its dimensions, producing a write outside the V8 sandbox. The final stage targeted Crashpad, which runs outside the renderer sandbox. A faulty memory-read retry could overflow a buffer when memory protections changed between reads, enabling code execution in the crash handler. The demonstration launched Windows Calculator from a webpage in Chrome Beta. For users, execution outside the browser’s sandbox could expose files and credentials or allow malware installation. Google’s public issue record confirms that an engineer reproduced the chain and that its vulnerability rewards panel approved the $250,000 payment on August 31. For comparison, exploit broker Crowdfense advertises payouts of up to $1.5 million for desktop Chrome zero-day chains, six times Google’s award. 6 days and $40,000 of compute with GPT-5.6 Sol to find a critical vulnerability in Chrome, claiming Google’s first full-chain reward in 2026 for a vulnerability that would affect an estimated 1 billion users.Highlights the opportunity for defenders to utilize these tools to… https://t.co/4q6AannOjN— Greg Brockman (@gdb) October 13, 2026 Human direction remained essential The AI agents searched source code, tested hypotheses, developed proofs of concept, and drafted exploit components. Researchers selected targets, checked results, and redirected the work. The team also designed interchangeable stages with backup vulnerabilities. That preparation allowed it to replace a component when another bug proved to have been reported already. The result illustrates how AI can accelerate expert-led vulnerability research, although XBOW’s prediction that agents could independently discover similar bugs within a year remains unproven. Chrome users should install available updates and relaunch the browser for them to take effect.
